source_text: Τοῦτο εὐθύνεται· τοῦτο δέχεται τὴν τῶν ἐνταῦθα πεπολιτευμένων ἀντίδοσιν. Καὶ τὰς ἀρετὰς δὲ ἡμέτερα κτήματα γινόμενα εὕροι τις ἂν, ὅταν ἐξ ἐπιμελείας συνυφανθῶσι τῇ φύσει· καὶ οὔτε ἐπὶ γῆς μοχθοῦντας ἡμᾶς ἀπολιμπάνειν ἐθέλουσιν, ἢν μὴ πρὸς βίαν αὐτὰς ἑκόντες ἀποδιώξωμεν ταῖς τῶν χειρόνων ἐπαγωγαῖς· ἐκεῖσέ τε ἐπειγομένων προ τρέχουσι, καὶ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις τὸν κτησάμενον συντάττουσι, καὶ λάμπουσι δι' αἰῶνος ὑπὸ τοῖς τοῦ κτίσαντος ὀφθαλμοῖς. Πλοῦτος δὲ, καὶ δυναστεία, καὶ περιφάνεια, καὶ τρυφὴ, καὶ πᾶς ὁ τοιοῦτος ὄχλος, ὁ καθ' ἡμέραν ἐκ τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀνοίας αὐξα νόμενος, οὔτε συμπροῆλθε πρὸς τὸν βίον ἡμῖν, οὔτε συναπῆλθέ τισιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῷ δικαίῳ πάλαι ῥηθὲν ἐπὶ παντὸς ἀνθρώπου πέπηγε καὶ κρατεῖ· Γυμνὸς ἐξῆλθον ἐκ κοιλίας μητρός μου, γυμνὸς καὶ ἀπ ελεύσομαι. Ὁ μὲν οὖν ἄριστα βουλευόμενος, τῆς ψυχῆς ὅτι μάλιστα φροντίσει, καὶ τοῦτο διὰ πάντων πειράσεται σώζειν εἰλικρινές τε καὶ γνήσιον· τῆς σαρκὸς δὲ ἢ λιμῷ τηκομένης, ἢ κρυμῷ καὶ θάλπει προσ παλαιούσης, ἢ νόσοις ἀλγυνομένης, ἢ πασχούσης τι παρά τινων βίαιον, ὀλίγον ποιήσεται τὸν λόγον, τὸ τοῦ Παύλου φωνῶν ἐφ' ἑκάστου τῶν δυσχερῶν, καὶ φθεγγόμενος· Εἰ καὶ ὁ ἔξωθεν ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος φθείρεται, ἀλλ' ὁ ἔσωθεν ἀνακαινοῦται ἡμέραν καθ' ἡμέραν. Καὶ οὔτε τοὺς ὑπὲρ τοῦ ζῇν κινδύνους προϊόντας ὁρῶν, φανήσεται δεδιὼς, ἀλλ' ἑαυτῷ λέξει θαῤῥῶν· Οἴδαμεν, ὅτι, ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος ἡμῶν οἰκία τοῦ σκήνους καταλυθῇ, οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ Θεοῦ ἔχο μεν, οἰκίαν ἀχειροποίητον, αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρα νοῖς. Εἰ δέ τις ἐθέλοι φείδεσθαι καὶ τοῦ σώματος, ὡς μόνου κτήματος ἀναγκαίου ψυχῇ, καὶ συνεργοῦν τος αὐτῇ πρὸς τὸ ζῇν ἐπὶ γῆς, μικρὰ πρὸς τὰς τού του χρείας ἐπιστραφήσεται, καὶ ὥστε συνέχειν μόνον αὐτὸ, καὶ τῇ τῆς ψυχῆς ὑπηρεσίᾳ διὰ μετρίας ἐπιμελείας ἐῤῥωμένον τηρεῖν, μὴ μέντοιγε ἐπιτρέπειν ὑπὸ κόρου σκιρτᾷν. Εἰ δὲ ἴδοι ποτὲ ταῖς τοῦ πλείονος καὶ πέρα τοῦ λυσιτελοῦντος ἐπιθυμίαις φλεγόμενον, βοήσει πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ τοῦ Παύλου νομοθετῶν· Οὐδὲν εἰσηνέγκαμεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον τοῦτον· δῆλον, ὅτι οὐδὲ ἐξενεγκεῖν τι δυνάμεθα. Ἔχοντες δὲ διατροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, τούτοις ἀρκεσθησόμεθα. Ταῦτα μὲν γὰρ ἐπᾴδων αὐτῷ συνεχῶς καὶ βοῶν, εὐήνιόν τε αὐτὸ καὶ κοῦφον ἀεὶ πρὸς τὴν οὐρά νιον ὁδοιπορίαν ἐργάσεται, καὶ μᾶλλον εἰς τὰ προκεί μενα κτήσεται συνεργόν· εἰ δὲ ὑβρίζειν αὐτὸ συγχωρήσοι, καὶ πάντων ἐφ' ἡμέραν ἐμπίπλασθαι, καθ άπερ τι θηρίον ἀνήμερον, ὕστερον ταῖς βιαίοις αὐτοῦ πρὸς γῆν ἀνθολκαῖς συνεπισπασθεὶς, κείσεται στέ νων ἀνόνητα. Καὶ πρὸς τὸν Δεσπότην ἀχθεὶς, καὶ τῆς ἐπὶ γῆς πορείας τῆς ἐνδοθείσης αὐτῷ τὸν καρπὸν ἀπαιτούμενος, εἶτα οὐκ ἔχων δοῦναι, θρηνή σει μακρὰ, καὶ σκότος οἰκήσει διηνεκὲς, πολλὰ τῇ τρυφῇ καὶ τῇ ταύτης πλάνῃ μεμφόμενος, ὑφ' ἧς τὸν τῆς σωτηρίας ἐσυλήθη καιρόν· οὐδὲν δὲ ἐκ τῶν δα κρύων ἔτι κερδαίνων. Ἐν γὰρ τῷ ᾅδῃ τίς ἐξομολογήσεταί σοι; φησὶν ὁ Δαβίδ. Φύγωμεν οὖν ὅπως ἔνι τάχους, μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἑκόντες συμπνίξωμεν. Εἰ δ' ἄρα τις καὶ πάλαι δελεασθεὶς, ἢ πλούτου κόνιν ἐξ ἀδικίας ἐφ' ἑαυτὸν συνεφόρησε, καὶ τὸν νοῦν ταῖς τούτου μερίμναις κατέδησεν, ἢ μύσος ἀσελγείας προσῆψε τῇ φύσει δυσέκνιπτον, ἢ τῶν ἄλλων ἐγκλημάτων ἐπλήρωσεν ἑαυτόν· οὗτος, ὡς ἔτι καιρὸς, πρὶν ἐλθεῖν εἰς τε λείαν ἀπώλειαν, ἀποθέσθω τῶν φορτίων τὰ πλείονα, καὶ πρὶν ὑποβρύχιον γενέσθαι τὸ σκάφος, ἐκβολὴν ποιησάσθω τῶν ἀγωγίμων, ἃ μὴ δεόντως συνέλεξε, καὶ μιμησάσθω τοὺς τῆς θαλάττης ἐργάτας.
thought_title: The soul's true possessions and the body's discipline
orientation: Basil is explaining what is truly ours—the soul, the body, and the virtues—and what is alien, namely wealth and luxury, which cannot follow us beyond death.
pass_a_gloss: This is set straight; this receives the recompense of those who have lived as citizens here. And the virtues one would find becoming our possessions, whenever from care they are woven together with nature; and neither while we toil on earth are they willing to leave us behind, unless we willingly drive them away by force through the inducements of worse things; and there, as we hasten, they run ahead, and they rank the one who acquired them with the angels, and they shine forever under the eyes of the Creator. But wealth, and power, and distinction, and luxury, and all such a crowd, which daily from our folly is increased, neither came forth with us into life, nor departed with anyone, but what was said long ago to the righteous man has been fixed and prevails over every human being: Naked I came out of my mother's womb, naked also I shall depart. The one therefore who plans best will care for the soul as much as possible, and this through all things he will try to keep pure and genuine; but of the flesh, whether wasting with hunger, or struggling with cold and heat, or pained by diseases, or suffering something violent from certain people, he will make little account, uttering the word of Paul at each of the difficulties, and saying: Even if our outer man is being destroyed, yet the inner man is being renewed day by day. And neither seeing the dangers for the sake of living coming on, will he appear afraid, but he will say to himself with confidence: We know that, if our earthly house of the tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. But if someone should wish to spare also the body, as the only necessary possession for the soul, and as cooperating with it for living on earth, he will turn a little to its needs, and so as only to hold it together, and to keep it strengthened for the service of the soul through moderate care, not however to allow it to leap about from satiety. But if he should ever see it inflamed with desires for more and beyond what is profitable, he will cry out to it, laying down the law of Paul: We brought nothing into this world; it is clear, that neither can we carry anything out. But having food and coverings, with these we shall be content. For by chanting these things to it continually and crying out, he will make it both obedient to the rein and light always for the heavenly journey, and rather he will acquire it as a helper for the things set before; but if he should allow it to run riot, and to be filled daily with all things, like some wild beast, later, dragged down together by its violent pulls toward the earth, he will lie groaning without profit. And brought before the Master, and being demanded the fruit of the earthly journey given to him, then not having to give, he will lament long, and will dwell in perpetual darkness, blaming much the luxury and its deception, by which he was robbed of the time of salvation; and gaining nothing further from the tears. For in Hades who will confess to you? says David. Let us flee therefore with all possible speed, lest we willingly choke ourselves. But if indeed someone, even long ago enticed, either heaped upon himself the dust of wealth from injustice, and bound his mind with its cares, or attached to his nature the hard-to-wash-off defilement of licentiousness, or filled himself with the other accusations; this man, while there is still opportunity, before coming to complete destruction, let him put off the greater part of the burdens, and before the vessel becomes submerged, let him make a jettison of the cargo, which he improperly collected, and let him imitate the workers of the sea.

choices.english: those who have lived as citizens here
choices.why: The verb πολιτεύομαι means to live as a citizen or conduct one's life; the perfect participle refers to those whose conduct of life has been completed in this world, and the rendering keeps the civic metaphor Basil uses for earthly life.
Basil uses ὄχλος contemptuously for the mass of worldly goods—wealth, power, distinction, luxury—as a disorderly mob; 'crowd' preserves the pejorative collective image.
The verb σκιρτάω describes the frisking or prancing of animals, especially when overfed; 'leap about' conveys the unruly bodily motion Basil warns against.
ἀνθολκή is a rare noun meaning a pulling against or toward; Basil uses it for the body's violent dragging of the soul down to earth, and 'pulls toward' keeps the directional force of the prefix ἀνθ-.
ἐκβολή is the technical nautical term for throwing cargo overboard to lighten a ship; 'jettison' preserves the maritime metaphor Basil develops with the workers of the sea.

μύσος means pollution or defilement, and ἀσέλγεια is licentiousness or wantonness; the phrase names a moral stain that clings to one's nature, and 'defilement of licentiousness' keeps both the stain and the specific vice.

pass_b_english: This is what is set straight; this is what receives the recompense for those who have lived as citizens here. And you would find that the virtues also become our possessions when they are woven together with our nature by our own care. They are not willing to leave us while we labor on earth, unless we ourselves willingly drive them away by the inducements of worse things. They run ahead of us as we press on to the other world, they rank their possessor together with the angels, and they shine forever under the eyes of their Creator. But wealth, and power, and distinction, and luxury, and all that sort of crowd that grows daily from our own folly—these did not come forth with us into life, nor have they departed with anyone. What was said long ago by the righteous man stands fixed and prevails over every human being: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will depart” (Job 1:21).

So the person who plans best will care for the soul as much as possible, and through everything will try to keep it pure and genuine. But if the flesh is wasting with hunger, or struggling against cold and heat, or pained by illnesses, or suffering something violent from others, he will make little account of it. In every hardship he will speak Paul’s words and say: “Even if our outer person is wasting away, yet our inner person is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). And when he sees dangers coming that threaten his life, he will not appear afraid, but will say to himself with confidence: “We know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

But if someone wishes to spare the body as well, as the one necessary possession of the soul and its fellow worker for living on earth, he will turn only a little attention to its needs—just enough to hold it together and keep it strong for the soul’s service through moderate care, but certainly not to allow it to leap about from being overfed. And if he ever sees it inflamed with desires for more than what is profitable, he will cry out to it, laying down Paul’s law: “We brought nothing into this world, and it is clear that we can carry nothing out. But if we have food and covering, with these we will be content” (1 Timothy 6:7-8).

For by chanting these words to it constantly and crying out, he will make it obedient to the rein and always light for the heavenly journey, and will gain it rather as a fellow worker for the things set before him. But if he allows it to run wild and to be filled with everything every day, like some untamed beast, he will later be dragged down with it by its violent pulls toward the earth, and will lie groaning to no profit. And when he is brought before the Master and asked for the fruit of the earthly journey that was given to him, and then cannot give it, he will lament at length and dwell in perpetual darkness, blaming luxury and its deception, by which he was robbed of the time of salvation—yet gaining nothing more from his tears. For “in the grave who will praise you?” says David (Psalm 6:5).

Let us flee, then, as quickly as possible, so that we do not willingly choke ourselves. But if someone was enticed long ago and heaped up the dust of wealth from injustice upon himself, and bound his mind with its cares, or attached to his nature a defilement of licentiousness that is hard to wash out, or filled himself with other accusations—let this person, while there is still time, before he comes to utter destruction, put off the greater part of his cargo. Before the vessel goes under the water, let him jettison the goods he gathered improperly, and let him imitate the workers of the sea.

last_rejected.quote: by the inducements of worse things
last_rejected.why: χειρόνων means 'of the hands' (i.e., manual pursuits/works), not 'of worse things'.
last_rejected.ruling: χειρόνων is genitive plural of χείρων ('worse'), not χείρ ('hand'); 'worse things' is correct.

last_rejected.quote: they rank their possessor together with the angels
last_rejected.why: συντάσσειν with dative means 'enroll/assign among', not 'rank together with'.
last_rejected.fix: they enroll their possessor among the angels
last_rejected.ruling: συντάττουσι here means 'rank/arrange with,' a normal sense; 'rank together with' captures the meaning accurately.

last_rejected.quote: he will cry out to it, laying down Paul’s law
last_rejected.source_quote: βοήσει πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ τοῦ Παύλου νομοθετῶν
last_rejected.why: The Greek says Paul is 'laying down the law' (νομοθετῶν), a participle describing Paul's action in the quotation. The English makes 'he' (the person) lay down Paul's law, changing who performs the action. The subject of βοήσει is the person, but νομοθετῶν describes Paul speaking authoritatively.
last_rejected.fix: he will cry out to it, with Paul legislating
last_rejected.ruling: νομοθετῶν can agree with the subject of βοήσει; the person cites Paul as lawgiver. Defensible reading, not a clear error.

last_rejected.why: 'εὐήνιον' means 'well-reined, manageable, tractable' - describing the body as easily guided. 'Obedient to the rein' is awkward and slightly off; the metaphor is of a horse responding to the rein, hence tractable or manageable.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Obedient to the rein' captures εὐήνιον's equestrian metaphor (εὖ + ἡνία). Within normal range; mere preference.
